positions.claim: An agent's identity is its log, not the model or the execution environment it runs in.
The log alone is sufficient to resume an agent, because the model, tools, and runtime only read from and append to it.
Everything else in an agent system — model context, UI, debugging, auditing, compaction — is a projection of the log, and only the log is not a projection.
Compaction is lossy and should be treated as a best-effort fork resumed as a new log, with the raw log retained.
The log cannot make the external world deterministic; side effects like sent emails or externally modified files are outside its scope, and that does not invalidate the thesis.
Claude Code loses a pending permission prompt if the process dies and the session is resumed, which is unacceptable in production.
Most agent harnesses run one process per agent, tying the agent to a specific machine; log-centric design removes sticky sessions, state migration, and coordination overhead.
Provider migration is only an adapter and schema problem, not an identity problem, if the log is the agent.
Claude Code and Codex write JSONL logs to local disk with fire-and-forget writes in SDK mode, so failed writes lose data; OpenCode's SQLite state has documented corruption and data-loss issues.
Log lock-in is a deeper and more durable form of vendor lock-in than model, API, or tool lock-in.
Every managed agent provider (Anthropic, Google) will move to own more of the stack — the hosted loop, memory, sandboxes, compaction, background agents.
Teams should self-host or otherwise fully own and inspect their agent logs rather than leaving them on a provider's infrastructure.
Real-world agent systems will inevitably face crashing workers, restarting machines, disappearing sandboxes, timed-out tool calls and failing providers, so durability must be architectural.
